title: Acceleration and Motion Graphs
competency: Identify that forces cause objects to accelerate, and that acceleration of an object is its rate of change of velocity; observe and describe examples of accelerating objects; and construct and annotate distance-time and velocity-time graphs to represent uniform and non-uniform acceleration.
objectives: Define acceleration and its relationship to force.
Calculate acceleration using the change in velocity over time.
Differentiate between uniform and non-uniform acceleration.
Interpret distance-time and velocity-time graphs for accelerating objects.
Describe uniform circular motion as a form of acceleration.
introduction: In the previous lessons, we discussed objects moving at a constant speed. However, most things in real life—like a car starting from a stoplight or a ball falling from a roof—change their speed or direction. This change in motion is called 'Acceleration,' and it only happens when an unbalanced force is applied.
content:
1. What is Acceleration?

Acceleration is the rate at which an object changes its velocity. Because velocity involves both speed and direction, an object accelerates if it:

  • Speeds up
  • Slows down (often called deceleration)
  • Changes direction

The formula for average acceleration is: a = (vf - vi) / t, where vf is final velocity, vi is initial velocity, and t is time. The standard unit is m/s² (meters per second squared).

2. Force and Acceleration

An object will only accelerate if an unbalanced force acts on it. According to the laws of physics, the greater the force applied to an object, the greater its acceleration will be.

3. Uniform Circular Motion

Even if an object is moving at a constant speed, it is still accelerating if it is moving in a circle. This is because its direction is constantly changing. Examples include a merry-go-round or a car turning a corner.

4. Graphing Acceleration

  • Distance-Time (d-t) Graph: Acceleration is represented by a curved line (parabola). A curve that gets steeper means the object is speeding up.
  • Velocity-Time (v-t) Graph: Acceleration is represented by the slope of the line.
    • A straight diagonal line means uniform (constant) acceleration.
    • A horizontal line means zero acceleration (constant velocity).
    • A curved line means non-uniform acceleration.

examples.title: Calculating Acceleration
examples.description: A car starts from rest (0 m/s) and reaches a velocity of 20 m/s in 4 seconds. Acceleration = (20 - 0) / 4 = 5 m/s².

examples.title: Athletes on an Oval
examples.description: A runner sprinting at a steady 5 m/s around a curved track is accelerating because their direction of travel is constantly changing as they follow the curve.

keyTerms.definition: The speed of an object in a particular direction.
A type of motion in which the velocity of an object changes by an equal amount in every equal time period.
The steepness of a line on a graph; on a v-t graph, it represents acceleration.

keyConcepts: Acceleration occurs whenever there is a change in speed, direction, or both.
Force is the cause of acceleration.
The area under a velocity-time graph represents the displacement of the object.
summary: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. It is caused by unbalanced forces and is measured in m/s². We can represent acceleration visually: a curved line on a distance-time graph and a sloped line on a velocity-time graph indicate that an object's motion is changing.

selfCheck.q: What is the standard unit used to measure acceleration?
If an object moves at a constant speed but changes direction, is it accelerating?
What does a horizontal line on a velocity-time graph represent?
